Oman Oil Terminal Attack Rattles the Market's Last Calm Corner
By Irina Slav - Jun 05, 2026, 12:26 AM CDT
Media reports about a blast disrupting oil loadings at Oman’s main terminal pushed benchmark prices higher earlier today, in the latest sign that any hopes about an end to Persian Gulf hostilities is probably premature.
At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $95.37 per barrel, and West Texas Intermediate was changing hands for $93.04 per barrel on the futures market, modestly up on Thursday, when prices dropped on reports about a ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah.
What makes the news significant is the fact that Oman is just outside the Strait of Hormuz and, as such, has seen a surge in interest from oil buyers, on the assumption that it will not be dragged into the hostilities.
Indeed, India earlier this week sealed a trade agreement with the Gulf state to secure oil imports that do not have to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. The country is heavily dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for its energy imports, with 45% of its crude oil purchases originating in the Persian Gulf, along with 55% of liquefied gas imports.
“Any optimism remains heavily clouded by a tangled web of headlines and counter-headlines,” IG analyst Tony Sycamore said in a note, as quoted by Reuters earlier today. “From a technical perspective, as long as (WTI) crude oil remains above trendline support in the low $80s, the risks remain skewed to the upside,” he added.

By TaiwanPlus

Taiwan's legislature has advanced four competing bills for funding drone acquisition plans to committee, marking the next stage in debate over how to expand the country's unmanned aerial capabilities. The Cabinet has proposed allocating nearly US$6.5 billion over five years to procure more than 200,000 drones.
Alternative proposals have also been submitted by the Kuomintang, the Taiwan People's Party and an individual Democratic Progressive Party lawmaker.
Drone Funding Bills

Lawmakers in Taiwan have voted to advance competing drone budget bills to committee for review.

candidates.snippet:
Executives and analysts say the draw is a manufacturing base that offers quality, cost and ease of collaboration, paired with Taiwan's own large appetite for military drones.
Interest in Taiwan's drone sector has surged over the past two years.
Its direct purchasing in Taiwan grew 15-fold over the same period, and it hired eight local employees.
The company's Altius-600M anti-armor drone, sold to Taiwan through the US Foreign Military Sales (FMS) program, went from contract signing to delivery in 13 months. It was Anduril's first overseas FMS case.
In February 2026, it signed a contract with NCSIST to integrate its Hivemind AI platform into Taiwan-developed unmanned systems, a step intended to move Taiwanese drones from autopilot toward autonomous decision-making.
Fang Yi-jan (方怡然), a national security policy analyst at DSET, said foreign drone makers are drawn by government tenders, Taiwan's supply chain and the prospect of combining software with hardware.
"Why are foreign companies interested in the Taiwan market? Because we have issued a tender, which is a very clear demand signal.
With heavy domestic demand for military drones, a deep manufacturing base and semiconductor strength, Taiwan now has major foreign backers. How far that will carry it toward becoming a global drone power remains to be seen.
This report is based on Storm Media's Chinese-language "Drone Myths" investigative series.

Destinus and the Netherlands Ministry of Defence launch Hornet B2 naval counter-UAS development program
A new Concept Development & Evaluation program will integrate Hornet B2 with Royal Netherlands Navy warships and develop the system towards a possible initial operating capability.
‍ Naval air defence faces an increasingly difficult economics problem.
Low-cost aerial threats can arrive in volume, and meeting each one with a premium interceptor is an equation no navy can sustain.
The Ministry of Defence’s Materiel and IT Command, COMMIT, has signed a contract with Destinus to launch a Concept Development & Evaluation program for a kinetic counter-UAS capability for the Royal Netherlands Navy.
A different approach to naval interception
Built with the operators from the start
“Low-cost aerial threats have inverted the economics of naval air defence: no navy can sustainably trade multimillion-euro missiles against low-cost threats arriving at volume,” said Mikhail Kokorich, CEO of Destinus.
“Hornet B2 answers this with a different architecture: launched from a canister like a missile, cruising on electric power like an aircraft, and engaging subsonic threats at a fraction of the cost per engagement.
Developing this capability together with COMMIT and the Royal Netherlands Navy from day one means it will be shaped by the operators who will depend on it.”
The program supports the Netherlands’ publicly stated requirement for a maritime kinetic counter-UAS capability for the fleet.

An oil tanker that violated Iranian transit rules caught fire after hitting a sea mine in the Strait of Hormuz, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of Iran said, Fars news agency reports.
According to the IRGC, the ship turned off its automatic identification system while passing through the strait, thus violating Iranian transit rules.
Iranian media had reported Monday about another incident involving another tanker that hit a mine in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC had informed that the shutdown of navigation and identification systems would be considered as a basis for taking strict and decisive measures against ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has announced its intention to present new targets and types of weapons, drawing attention to seven major underwater internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz.
Statement on cables and weapons
Mohebbi said that seven main internet cables run beneath the Strait of Hormuz. According to him, all internet and commercial data traffic passes through them.
The IRGC spokesperson also said that Iran would present new targets and new types of weapons.
Previous statements by Tehran
Earlier in October, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told state broadcaster Press TV that Tehran could strike underwater internet cables, data centers and artificial intelligence facilities linked to the United States in the event of a new war.
He noted that these facilities had not yet been included on the list of targets, but warned that they could be destroyed if the conflict resumed.
As Anadolu Agency writes, the United States and Israel began a war against Iran on February 28, after which Tehran responded with missile and drone strikes across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
In June, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum on freedom of navigation in the strait, but its implementation was halted due to disputes over security on this strategic waterway.

candidates.snippet:
What bringing your own power solves
Idle GPUs cost far more than the electricity to run them, so speed matters most — what folks call “time to power.” That’s why developers are planning to bring their own power on site (“behind the meter”), but almost always alongside a connection to the grid, or as a bridge to one:
* Pecos County: Pacifico describes its planned microgrid (a behind-the-meter setup) at GW Ranch as never drawing from ERCOT , yet the site’s new owner, Amazon, says it’s designed to join the grid once it can connect.
SemiAnalysis is already tracking 75 GW of equipment orders for behind-the-meter assets, but every site I’m aware of intends to connect to the grid as soon as it can, chiefly because on-site power almost always costs more. So, once the grid is available, say in year five, you switch.
Expect more batteries and other energy storage as rack-level power density grows and swings become more dramatic.
Then there’s fueling a site. Winter Storm Uri’s lesson is that gas plants can fail together . And since they tend to keep little fuel on site (NERC calls gas a “just-in-time” fuel ), spare turbines don’t always help.
Thus, behind-the-meter setups favor modularity, like the more than 500 gas engines of about 4 MW each planned for Shackelford, though hundreds of engines can be a pain to maintain.
Full reliability for an island is very, very hard, but some labs and hyperscalers have shown that, forced to choose between reliability and speed, they’ll pick speed.

Leaderdrive harmonic reducers and the humanoid market
Founded in 2011 by Zuo Yuyu, Leaderdrive focuses on affordable robot components and has become China’s largest manufacturer of harmonic reducers. These precision gear systems function as joints in robotic arms and humanoid machines, making them a central part of the motion stack for many robot designs.

Research firm Omdia said global humanoid robot shipments rose nearly 480% in 2025 to 13,318 units, and projected that figure would reach 2.6 million units by 2035. Even if forecasts at that horizon remain uncertain, they help explain why component makers tied to actuation and motion control are attracting more attention from investors.

* Microgrids Military & Defense News

Key Facts
* Reactors range from 1 MW to 20 MW and are contractor-owned and contractor-operated
* At least one reactor must be operational by September 30, 2028
The US Army selected five companies on August 26 to build nuclear microreactors at five installations. The agreements are worth up to $2.2 billion through fiscal 2031. The program is called Janus.
Fuel choices differ across the group. Radiant and Antares plan to use HALEU in TRISO form. General Atomics plans uranium zirconium hydride. Jeff Waksman, the Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment, leads the effort on the Army side.
The Army frames Janus as energy independence.
A 1 MW to 20 MW generator that runs for years without refueling is a microgrid asset, not a power plant. Diesel gensets and batteries carry most installations through an outage today. Both depend on fuel deliveries or on a short discharge window. A reactor sized to a base changes the resilience math, because the fuel is already on site.
They do not speed up the licensing.
Milestone-based payment protects the money, not the timeline. If Antares, BWXT, General Atomics, Radiant and Westinghouse all slip together, the Army has spent little and gained nothing on schedule. The resilience claim needs a test as well.
